newsitem.title: MALAYSIA: FOCUS-Asian stock markets mixed after baht float.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Asian stock markets mixed after baht float.

text.p: The flotation of Thailand's currency prompted a relieved rally in its beleaguered stock market on Wednesday but drew mixed reactions from other Asian bourses more focused on domestic issues, analysts said.
At midday, the Thailand composite SET stock index was up 40.93 points, or 7.76 percent, to 568.21, close to its 568.54 session high for the day.

The Thai stock market barometer initially dropped 1.1 percent at the open in reaction to news that the exchange rate system would be changed to a managed float instead of set against a basket of currencies dominated by the U.S. dollar.

"It's what everybody's been waiting for," said a Thailand-based foreign analyst when asked about the market's reversal. Rumours had been swirling in markets for months that the baht may be devalued against the backdrop of the slowest economic growth in Thailand in a decade.
"I don't think the float will spill over into the region," said Ng Bok Eng, regional economist at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell in Singapore.
Indeed, the enthusiasm did not spread evenly to Thailand's neighbours. Malaysia, just to the south, gained, but Manila shares dropped, Indonesia saw a record rise and Singapore eased.
Other stock markets posting gains in the region included Seoul, Tokyo, Bombay and Australia. But the reasons for the gains were as varied as the extent of the rises.
South Korean shares closed up 2.54 percent, or 19.26 points, to 777.29 on broad optimism about an economic recovery.

Australian stocks notched a record close, with the All Ordinaries Index leaping 24.7 points to 2,745.9. Brokers were pleased but slightly bewildered as to the factors driving the latest uptick in the market's bull run.
In Tokyo, shares added 20.90 points, or 0.10 percent, to close at 20,196.42, helped in part by bargain-hunting, brokers said.
Hong Kong's stock market was closed for a three-day holiday marking the territory's return to Chinese rule. It reopens on Thursday.
The Bombay index was up 56.36 points, or 1.31 percent, to 4357.22 at noon after hitting a 20-month high on Tuesday. Heavy foreign fund buying has been boosting the market.
In Malaysia, the Composite Index of 100 blue chips gained 3.36 points, or 0.31 percent, to 1,082.26 as of 0725 GMT, with players taking their cue more from the stable ringgit than the Thai baht news.
On the minus side, the Philippines' composite index closed down 1.8 percent to 2,764.89 as wild swings in the foreign exchange market spooked investors.

Earlier in the day, the Philippine Central Bank offered one-day reverse repo at 20 percent and later raised it to 24 percent to curb a speculative attack on the peso. It also sold millions of dollars to defend the local currency following Thailand's announcement on the baht.
"Everyone's banking on the Central Bank to contain this latest shocker...due to the Thai crisis," said Joey Roxas, president of Eagle Securities Inc in Manila.

The Jakarta Composite Index slipped 3.27 points, or 0.45 percent, to 728.363 points in the afternoon after hitting a record high of 734.02 earlier. Buying by an increasing number of domestic mutual funds has helped to boost the market, analysts said.
"I don't see any direct impact of the Thai baht in the Jakarta stock market today," said Naotaka Ikeda, director of Asian Development Securities brokerage in Indonesia.
Shanghai's foreign currency B shares dropped 3.08 percent to 78.971 in early Wednesday afternoon trading, dragged down by a plunge on the domestic A share market.
In Taiwan, the key stock index sank 33.56 points, or 0.37 percent, to 8,996.72, dragged lower by selling on electronics shares.
Singapore's Straits Times Industrials Index dropped 9.00 points, or 0.45 percent.
